strategies.blurb: No AI forecast: on games, it buys a Kalshi or Polymarket side priced at least 3¢ below Pinnacle's odds with the bookmaker's margin taken out. strategies.name: favorites
strategies.label: Heavy favorites, big bets (for fun)

On 239 past markets that rule won 95% of its bets and came out about even after fees (-0.5% a bet, range -3.7% to +2.3%). Expect lots of small wins and the odd big loss.

recent.question: Will the Democratic Party win the SC-01 House seat?
recent.what_happened: Democrat Nancy Lacore won the open SC-01 seat on Nov 3, 2026. Unofficial returns had her at 49.65% to Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt's 48.64%, a margin of about 3,300 votes. Honeycutt conceded, which flipped the seat to the Democrats.
recent.what_we_missed: The polls we had showed a close race: Honeycutt led by only 1 to 6 points, and her biggest lead (+6) came from a Republican-aligned pollster. The national mood also favored Democrats, with a midterm under a Republican president, an unpopular Iran war and tariffs, and Lacore was a strong, well-funded candidate. Still, the research-based forecast leaned on the R+6 partisan lean and the 'solid R' label and went down to 14%. That was well below the market's 30.5% and below our own no-research forecast of 34%.
recent.lesson: When polls of an open seat show a single-digit race and the national environment favors the challenger's party, don't let the district's partisan lean pull the probability far below the market. In an open-seat midterm, an R+6 seat can easily swing that much.

suggested_change.change: Flag forecasts that sit more than about 15 points below the market when the latest polls are within the margin of error, and require stated reasons before the forecast can go out.

recent.question: Will the Republican Party win the SC-01 House seat?
recent.what_happened: Democrat Nancy Lacore flipped SC-01, beating Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt about 49.65% to 48.64% in unofficial results, just over South Carolina's recount threshold. Honeycutt conceded on Nov 4. Coverage credits Lacore's gains in Berkeley and Dorchester counties, her fundraising edge and a midterm climate that favored Democrats.
recent.what_we_missed: The evidence pointed to a toss-up. Both Democratic-aligned polls had Honeycutt up only 1–2 points, the one Republican pollster had her up 6, and Lacore outraised her by a wide margin. On top of that, the open seat in a midterm under a Republican president with tariffs and the Iran war as issues looked like 2018, when Cunningham flipped this seat. Research moved the forecast up from 0.52 to 0.73 by leaning on the Republican-aligned co/efficient poll and on a 'solidly Republican' label. Cook actually rated the race 'Likely R', and its R+6 lean is a historical figure, not a reading of this race.
recent.lesson: In an open-seat race during a midterm, when nonpartisan or opposite-party polling shows a lead of 3 points or less, keep the probability near 50–65%. Partisan lean indexes and polls from the favored party's own pollsters shouldn't push it higher.

suggested_change.change: Weight polls by sponsor, average them so the effect of partisan pollsters cancels out, and check race ratings against the primary source (Cook, Sabato, Inside Elections). Don't rely on secondhand labels like 'solidly Republican'.

recent.question: Bank of England increases interest rates by 25 bps after November 2026 meeting?
recent.what_happened: On 5 November 2026 the BoE raised Bank Rate 25bp to 4.00% by an 8–1 vote; Mann wanted 50bp. Bailey said energy-driven inflation pressure in the pipeline now justified a hike. September CPI had risen to 3.5%, and analysts widely expected the move.
recent.what_we_missed: By 7 October the market was pricing a hike at about 91.5%, so information beyond the 17 September minutes had probably moved expectations, such as later MPC speeches or OIS pricing. The research stopped at the September meeting, read the 6–3 hold majority as dovish, and missed that Bailey's 'insurance hike' framing plus Brent holding above $100 made a hike close to the default.
recent.lesson: When a central-bank market sits at an extreme like 90% or more and the forecast is near 50%, look up current OIS or futures pricing and policymaker speeches since the last meeting before departing sharply from the market.

suggested_change.change: For central-bank rate questions, always fetch current market-implied probabilities (OIS or SONIA futures) and any MPC member speeches since the last meeting, and record them as facts.

recent.question: Will the Democrats win the Ohio governor race in 2026?
recent.what_happened: Democrat Amy Acton won the Ohio governor's race, resolving the question YES. She had led almost every high-quality poll in early October (CNN/SSRS +8, NYT/Siena +4, Marist +6, Suffolk +9, YouGov +4), and prediction markets had her at roughly 68–80%. My search didn't find post-election coverage, so the YES result comes from the outcome given, not from results I checked.
recent.what_we_missed: The forecaster put Acton at 42%, below even odds, despite a consistent poll lead, Toss-up ratings, and a 67.5% market. It leaned too hard on one outlet's informal comparison of four past races, where polls understated Republicans in presidential and Senate contests. It also gave too much weight to Ohio's partisan lean and to a single Republican-leaning co/efficient poll, and missed that this was a midterm with a weak Republican nominee and a polling lead that was growing.
recent.lesson: If nearly every high-quality poll and the market agree on a leader, an informal polling-error adjustment drawn from a few presidential-year races should shrink the lead, not reverse it. Forecasting below 50% against the poll leader needs strong, race-specific evidence.

suggested_change.change: Flag for review any forecast that puts the consensus poll leader below 50% while the market is above 60%, and require the forecaster to show that its polling-bias adjustment is based on similar elections (midterm, governor race) rather than presidential races.

recent.question: Will the Democrats win the South Carolina Senate race in 2026?
recent.what_happened: Democrat Annie Andrews beat appointed Sen. Darline Graham, who replaced her late brother Lindsey Graham, on Nov. 3, 2026. AP, NBC and Fox all called the race for Andrews. It was the first Democratic Senate win in South Carolina since 1998. Polls tightened late, and a late-October NYT/Siena poll had the race tied at 48%.
recent.what_we_missed: As of Oct. 11, every recent poll had the race within 1 to 5 points, and the Republican was a weakened, newly appointed nominee coming off a bitter runoff. The 2020 Harrison precedent, where polls overstated the Democrat, may have been given too much weight in a cycle where conditions looked different. Our 20% was above the market's 15.5% but probably still too low.
recent.lesson: If a deep-red state has a weak or new incumbent and polls show a steady tie across several pollsters, including Republican-leaning ones, don't discount the Democrat's chances below about 25–30% on the strength of one past polling miss.

suggested_change.change: Check how the nominee's situation (appointed, after a runoff, no electoral record of their own) and the national climate this cycle differ from the past polling-error case, instead of applying that case's polling error wholesale.

recent.question: Will the Republicans win the South Carolina Senate race in 2026?
recent.what_happened: Democrat Annie Andrews beat appointed Sen. Darline Graham on Nov 3, 2026. AP, NBC and Decision Desk HQ all called the race within about three hours of polls closing, and Graham got roughly 47.2%. In the final weeks the polls had tightened to a tie, with NYT/Siena at 48–48.
recent.what_we_missed: We treated the 2020 polling miss and South Carolina's deep-red history as if they would reliably push Graham to a win. But she was a first-time candidate, appointed after her brother died, who only narrowly won the special runoff (52.5%). She never led in any poll by more than 1–5 points, and raters were moving the race toward Democrats. All of that pointed to real risk of a Democratic win, not just polling noise in a safe seat.
recent.lesson: If a weak or unusual candidate (appointed, first-time, or a surprise nominee) is tied in several independent polls, don't assume a past polling error will repeat. Keep the probability closer to 60–70%, even in a strongly partisan state.

suggested_change.change: Before adjusting for past polling bias, check whether the earlier error came from a different, stronger candidate. Then reduce the adjustment when the current nominee has no electoral track record or the circumstances are unusual.

recent_wins.question: Wild Horse Nine Rotten Tomatoes score? (Above 90)
recent_wins.what_happened: Martin McDonagh's Wild Horse Nine opened wide on Nov 6, 2026 and settled at about 93–94% on the Tomatometer with 100–130+ reviews, plus a Certified Fresh rating. That is above 90, so the question resolved YES. Its early festival scores were lower (87% on 15 reviews, then 90% on 39), but it rose as more reviews came in.
recent_wins.what_worked: The win came from the 'favorites' strategy buying the market favorite at 0.835, not from our own forecast. jev_alone said 0.3, which was badly wrong. By judgment time the film already had strong festival reviews and a score at or above 90, and the market had priced that in correctly. A prestige auteur film that is already over 90 on dozens of reviews rarely falls below 90 by wide release.
recent_wins.lesson: For Rotten Tomatoes strike questions, look up the current Tomatometer and review count before forecasting. A prestige film already at or above the strike with 30+ festival reviews usually holds or rises, so don't fade a market at 80%+ without looking.

suggested_change.change: Before any Tomatometer forecast, require a lookup of the current score and review count (which was missing here, since the fact list was empty), and flag any jev_alone estimate that differs from the market by more than 40 points with no supporting facts.

recent_wins.question: Will OpenAI release Astra 6.1 before Nov 6, 2026? (Before Nov 6, 2026)
recent_wins.what_happened: OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra on Sep 3, 2026, then released GPT-6.1 Sol at DevDay on Sep 29. Around that time it called off the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra after testing found a safety regression (reported by the WSJ). No Astra 6.1 came out before Nov 6, so the question resolved NO.
recent_wins.what_worked: With no research facts at all, the forecaster leaned NO at 25%. That was reasonable given how short the window was after Astra 6's early-September launch, and it fit how OpenAI tends to ship a cheaper variant (6.1 Sol) before a flagship point release. The market at 9.5% was better calibrated, though. It had evidently already priced in the reported cancellation, which our forecaster never saw.
recent_wins.lesson: For questions about a named model version, search the exact product name together with 'cancel', 'delay' or 'scrapped' and check recent event coverage (like DevDay) before forecasting. Here a public cancellation report would have justified going well below 25%.

suggested_change.change: If a forecast would otherwise go out with no facts, run at least one targeted news search for postponement or cancellation reports on the named product, so we don't sit at a vague base rate while the market already knows the deciding news.

recent_wins.question: US x Iran ceasefire continues through October 31?
recent_wins.what_happened: The United States made no qualifying air or missile strike on Iranian territory between October 11 and October 31, 2026, so the market resolved YES. Over that stretch there were attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, the US naval blockade continued, Qatar mediated indirect talks, and Iran threatened retaliation. Critical Threats' October 31 update listed nothing significant under US military operations.
recent_wins.what_worked: The forecaster had no researched facts and leaned on persistence: the shaky truce had mostly held since the July–August flare-ups, and only about 20 days were left. Both sides were tense but talking, so a US strike on Iranian soil in that short window was unlikely. Its 0.72 was right in direction but less confident than the market's 0.785, so it gained little over the market.
recent_wins.lesson: For short-window 'ceasefire continues' markets, start from how long the current lull has lasted and how much time remains. Don't mark below the market because of maritime incidents or threats; the rules explicitly exclude those, and only strikes that hit Iranian soil count.

suggested_change.change: Before forecasting, pull the latest conflict tracker (for example the Critical Threats Iran Update) to confirm when the last qualifying strike on Iranian land happened, so the forecast rests on evidence rather than a no-information prior.

recent_wins.question: Will the Democrats win the Iowa governor race in 2026?
recent_wins.what_happened: Democrat Rob Sand ran for Iowa's open governor seat against Republican Zach Lahn, who had upset the Trump-endorsed Randy Feenstra in the GOP primary. Before the election Sand led in polls, Kalshi priced him around 86% and some raters had the race leaning Democratic. The question resolved YES with Sand winning, though my searches didn't find the actual vote count.
recent_wins.what_worked: The money was made by the 'favorites' strategy, which bet $95 on YES because the market priced Democrats at 88.5%. Our own forecast had no research facts behind it and gave only 36%, which ignored Sand's polling lead and Lahn's weakness after the primary upset. The model's probability was wrong, and the profit came from following the market.
recent_wins.lesson: When the forecaster has no research facts and lands more than 40 points from a liquid market, assume the market knows something specific, such as a nominee change or polling, and find out what before trusting the model's prior that Iowa leans Republican.

suggested_change.change: When jev_with_research is missing and jev_alone is more than 30 points away from the market price, block contrarian bets and either run research or defer to the market.

recent_wins.question: Will there be no Hormuz agreement?
recent_wins.what_happened: The market resolved to 'No Hormuz Agreement', meaning no qualifying US–Iran Hormuz deal was announced by Nov 2, 2026. My searches turned up only uncertain mid-June 2026 reports of an interim 'Islamabad MOU' on reopening the strait. Some came from questionable sites, and the reports disagreed on whether it had been formally signed. With the market at 0.83 'No' in October, traders were evidently not treating that MOU as a qualifying announcement accepted by both sides, and nothing new appears to have emerged in the final weeks.
recent_wins.what_worked: Not much from jev. It gave only 0.37 on the outcome that happened and had no research facts, so it was well on the wrong side of a market that already priced 'No' at 0.83. The win came from the 'favorites' strategy, which bet on the market's favorite. With three weeks left and no deal in sight, sticking with the status quo was the obvious call.
recent_wins.lesson: If an agreement has to be announced by a near deadline (here three weeks away), the market is at 0.83 for 'no deal', and you have no research showing a deal is imminent, don't put your forecast far below the market.

suggested_change.change: Block or shrink a forecast that sits more than 30 points from the market when there are no research facts behind it, especially on status-quo questions close to their deadline.

recent_wins.question: Will the Republicans win the Florida Senate race in 2026?
recent_wins.what_happened: Republican Ashley Moody won the November 3, 2026 Florida Senate special election. The AP called it on election night, and with about 99% of the expected vote counted NBC had her at roughly 50.9% to 48.0% over Democrat Angie Nixon. That is about a 3-point margin, much closer than Florida's R+10 lean.
recent_wins.what_worked: With research, the forecast moved from 0.45 to 0.78. That move came from structural facts: Florida's R+10.3 baseline, Republican wins in every Florida Senate race since 2012, and Moody's money advantage, which came to roughly 30x in cash on hand. Its other premise was that Florida polls understate Republicans by 7 to 8 points, and that did not hold this time. Moody beat Nixon by less than her lead in the September polls, so the call was right, but some of the reasoning behind it was wrong.
recent_wins.lesson: In a state with a strong partisan lean, base rates and the fundamentals should anchor the forecast. Don't assume past polling misses will repeat in the same direction, especially in a midterm where conditions may favor the other party, because this race came in near or below what the polls showed.

suggested_change.change: Add the national midterm environment (generic ballot and the president's approval rating) to the research, and use it to weigh how much past polling misses in a state should carry over. Leaning on the 2022 and 2024 Florida misses here overstated Moody's likely margin.

rules.rule: For price-touch questions (crypto, oil, commodities), copy strike, venue and test (touch or candle close) from the rules, check venue candles for a prior hit, and report spot within 15 min, % to strike, days left, volatility, days of last 14 through it, dated catalysts.

When a question resolves on an official statement, search for statements dated in the last 24 hours, and report independent dated reports that the event (e.g. pipeline flows) already happened plus the same body's past announcements of similar events and their lag.

For ceasefire or 'no strike' questions, read what counts as a breach (e.g. strikes on territory only, not ships or threats), check the latest dated conflict tracker (e.g. Critical Threats) for the last qualifying strike, and report the lull's length, days left and deployments.

For election questions, report the state's lean, recent results for the same office, cash on hand, every dated poll with pollster and sponsor, a nonpartisan-poll average, first-hand Cook/Sabato/Inside Elections ratings, other races' polls, primary turnout, national mood.

Before citing a past polling miss, check it was the same candidate and cycle type; report the nominee's own record and whether the seat is open; label partisan lean indexes, secondhand 'safe' labels, party-sponsored polls, win streaks and spending gaps as weak.

For match or fight questions, report both sides' dated absences, returns and weigh-in news, the stand-in's and absent player's recent output, settled from confirmed lineups; label head-to-heads under about 10 games, win streaks and common-opponent links as weak.

For team win, spread or total questions, report home-only and road-only records, dated scores and points allowed over each side's last 5, last 8–10 meetings, schedule strength, starting QB or key starter changes, and whether a draw resolves No; label 3–4 game streaks weak.

If a game, stage, final or ceremony began before judgment, first get its result from a source timestamped within the hour (league site, Liquipedia), dropping undated snippets; else report series wins needed, remaining rounds and opponents, or the award shortlist.

For tennis completion questions, read which endings count, report the tour level's normal-finish share and each player's recent full matches, weigh only past-week injury or withdrawal news, and after start time check Tennis Explorer or ITF for w/o or ret. first.

For NFL player props, research the named player, never team D/ST rates: for TDs, his TDs per game this and last season, red-zone carries or targets and target share; for yardage, attempts per game and games past the line; plus the opponent's rank and injured defenders.

For single MLB games, report confirmed starters' ERA, ERA+ and recent starts, each bullpen's unavailable arms (injury, leave, short rest), season and road records, and form since Sept 1; label old-roster franchise streaks and series-level rates as not single-game evidence.

For video view questions, check the channel's uploads since the question opened and report any new video's upload time, hours elapsed, views and climb rate first; build references only from first-168-hour counts of recent comparable uploads, not lifetime or undated totals.

For live-streamed challenge questions near the deadline, get the current attempt's status from the past 12 hours (stream VODs, streamers' socials, fan trackers): milestones reached, gear, deaths or resets, plus the participants' own past completions and times.

For Rotten Tomatoes score questions, read the year-specific film page named in the rules, record the score, review count and dated earlier readings showing drift, and count how many negative reviews would move it past the strike before the check time.

For reality-show elimination questions, confirm every fact names the asked contestant and their own pro partner, and report couples left, eliminations per episode, live shows in the window, and every couple's judges' scores and bottom-three history.

For cumulative box-office questions, take the latest weekend and daily totals from The Numbers or Box Office Mojo dated within 7 days of judgment, report recent weekly drop rates, and project the remaining gross to the deadline against the threshold.

For earnings-beat questions, copy the EPS basis (GAAP diluted or adjusted) and strike from the rules, report the dated consensus and recent revisions, the last 4–8 quarters' actual-versus-consensus surprise percentages, and management's dated guidance or segment commentary.

For CPI questions, get the dated consensus and Cleveland Fed nowcast, rebuild the 12-month rate from NSA index levels incl. the month dropping out, find the monthly change the strike needs, and estimate it bottom-up: gas weight × AAA/EIA change plus typical core and food.

For GDP questions, confirm the rules' threshold and measure (BEA advance estimate, annualized real growth) match the question title, then report the release date, the latest dated GDPNow and NY Fed nowcasts, each one's typical error, and recent quarters' nowcast misses.

For central-bank rate questions (Fed, BoE, ECB), take the current rate and last move from the latest statement and minutes, check the strike under the rules' exact wording, and report dated policymaker speeches since then, latest CPI, energy prices, dissents, economist polls.

ideas_for_joey.title: Break results down by price paid
ideas_for_joey.why: Many losses, including all 3 of claude_direct's and every info-gate-stopped group, show -$100 per $100, meaning the whole stake was lost. That pattern suggests we may be buying cheap longshots. A breakdown of wins and P&L by ask price (for example <0.2, 0.2–0.5, 0.5–0.8, >0.8), for placed and stopped bets, would let us set min_ask and max_ask from evidence instead of guessing.

ideas_for_joey.title: Shrink forecasts toward the market before computing edge
ideas_for_joey.why: The market's Brier (0.123, 201 markets) beats every forecaster, and most of our losses came from bets where we disagreed with it most, such as long shots that went 1 for 21. A strategy option that blends the forecast with the market price (for example 50/50) before the edge check would bet only where a disagreement survives that discount. The forecasters themselves would still never see the price.
